events.title: Delegates Sign the Declaration of Independence
events.description: Months after Congress voted for independence, delegates gathered in Philadelphia to sign the engrossed parchment copy of the Declaration of Independence. Most of the 56 signers added their names at this ceremony.
events.significance: The signing turned a statement of principles into a personal pledge. Each signer risked being charged with treason against the British Crown.

events.title: The First U.S. Census Begins
events.description: Federal marshals on horseback began counting the young republic's population. They recorded nearly 3.9 million people.
events.significance: The Constitution required a census, and this was the first. The count set a model for apportioning political representation that the U.S. still follows every ten years.

events.title: Einstein Signs His Letter to Roosevelt
events.description: Albert Einstein signed a letter, drafted with physicist Leo Szilard, warning President Franklin D. Roosevelt that Nazi Germany might build atomic weapons. The letter urged the United States to start its own research.
events.significance: The letter helped set in motion American atomic research, which grew into the Manhattan Project and ushered in the nuclear age.

events.title: PT-109 Is Sunk and Treblinka Prisoners Revolt
events.description: In the Pacific, a Japanese destroyer rammed and sank the patrol boat PT-109, commanded by Lt. John F. Kennedy. He helped lead his surviving crew to safety. The same day, prisoners rose up in the Nazi death camp at Treblinka.
events.significance: Kennedy's survival story later became a pillar of his political image. The Treblinka uprising was an act of desperate courage, and it helped lead to the camp's closure.
